check: One worktree per concurrent writer (the existing concurrent-dispatch worktree protocol) closes both the staging-collision and reset-hazard paths; strict path partitioning (git add <exact paths>) alone does not prevent a reset from one agent moving HEAD past another's just-landed commit.

source_anchor: OPS-46 — Simulating a credential's absence with a config flag, instead of removing it, gives a false negative
instance: Testing whether a stale registry credential caused ghcr.io pull failures by running `docker --config <empty-dir> pull` and `DOCKER_CONFIG=<empty-dir> docker pull` both still returned 'denied: denied', identical to the failure with the stale credential present, while curl with an anonymously-obtained bearer token returned 200 for the same manifest — read as evidence of a second, non-credential problem, when actually the isolation flag never severed the credential path at all; a real `docker logout ghcr.io` made anonymous pulls succeed immediately. The founder was asked to mint an unneeded classic PAT before this was found.
check: To test whether X causes a failure, remove X and confirm the removal took effect, then retest — don't substitute a flag or alternate config believed to bypass X; when two clients disagree about the same endpoint, suspect the client's credential resolution before concluding the endpoint is at fault.

source_anchor: OPS-47 — Measurements taken against a stale checkout report numbers that do not transfer
instance: A per-test timing profile and a '72% faster' A/B result were presented as properties of current code, but the working tree was a detached HEAD 90 commits behind main (13 test files/246 tests vs main's 20 files/373 tests) — git status reported a clean tree either way, so cleanliness was mistaken for currency. The same error recurred later in the session when an ID-allocation scan in the stale checkout reported the highest OPS-* id as 36 when main was already at 45.
check: Resolve the ref explicitly before any measurement or ID allocation (`git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main`) and run from a fresh worktree of origin/<default> rather than the ambient checkout; treat a long-lived repo root in a multi-worktree estate as stale by default.

source_anchor: OPS-48 — Editing the tree under an in-flight measurement silently contaminates its baseline
instance: An A/B baseline arm and treatment arm were launched in the same worktree; the treatment's one-line edit to dispatch/test/helpers.bash was applied while the baseline was mid-suite, and since bats re-sources helpers per test, every baseline test not yet reached silently ran with the treatment applied — nothing errored and no output flagged it, producing a plausible, wrong number.
check: Each arm of a comparison gets its own worktree, pinned to its own ref, created before either starts; never edit a path any running job reads, and discard a run rather than reasoning about which tests an in-flight edit reached.

source_anchor: OPS-49 — Infrastructure applied while its manifest sits on an unpushed branch
instance: helm upgrade was run against all affected ARC scale sets after a values change was committed locally but never pushed, so the cluster ran minRunners:1/maxRunners:6 while origin/main still declared the inherited 0/3 — the transcript offered the push as optional ('say the word and I'll push it'). A second instance the same session: a `parallel` line landed in the runner-image Dockerfile with no corresponding build, so the deployed fleet3 image no longer reproduced from main even though the pin and cluster agreed.
check: Push (or land) the manifest before applying, treating the push as the primary artifact and the apply as its consequence; verify by diffing declared vs. live explicitly across every affected object in both directions (cluster ahead of manifest, and manifest ahead of the built artifact) rather than inferring convergence from apply success.

source_anchor: CI-18 — A verification that the unfixed baseline also passes is reported as proof of the fix
instance: "the flake is fixed — it passed 20 consecutive runs" — when the *original* code also passes 20 consecutive runs in the same conditions. the check has no discriminating power: run the pre-fix version under the identical conditions and it passes too. Measured here: the fixed liveness test passed 15/15 on a quiet machine — and so did the unmodified `origin/main` version (15/15), plus 10/10 under synthetic CPU load. The only condition that ever reproduced the failure was real concurrent-agent load (10/12 failures). A repeat-count verification run outside that condition proves nothing about either version. repeating a test is mistaken for controlling the variable that makes it fail. For a load-dependent or environment-dependent defect, iteration count is the wrong axis entirely.
check: before accepting a fix for an intermittent failure, **measure the unfixed baseline under the same conditions** and require it to fail. If the baseline passes, the verification is void — say so rather than reporting the pass. State the reproduction condition explicitly in the brief (here: concurrent agent load, not CPU saturation) so the verifier reproduces the failure rather than the environment where it hides.

source_anchor: CI-19 — An acceptance predicate that has never matched a known-positive passes vacuously (false-green gate)
instance: a predicate used as a gate — a glob, a grep, a check script — is believed to be discriminating (pass on good, fail on bad) merely because it runs clean and returns 0. three same-day instances from the 2026-07-31 engram-disconnect campaign, each caught only by adversarial review, never by the predicate itself: (1) `~/bin/engram*` glob silently missing `merge-engram-chain.sh`, so the intended script was never on the matched set; (2) `rg 'a\|b'` where `\|` is a **literal pipe character**, not regex alternation — the pattern matches nothing, ever; (3) `rg` invoked without `--hidden` returning `0` over `.claude` dot-directories where the true count was 20. In all three, the predicate had never once been exercised against a case it should catch — a vacuous truth (no matches attempted = no failures observed) was read as a clean pass.
check: before any predicate is adopted as a gate, demonstrate it **matches a known-positive fixture** — its own RED proof: construct or point at an input the predicate must reject/catch, run the predicate, and confirm it actually fires. A predicate that has never been shown to match anything is unverified, not passing. Applies to globs, `rg`/`grep` patterns (watch escaped-metacharacter and `--hidden`/dotfile traps specifically), file-existence checks, and any other acceptance/gate condition.

source_anchor: CI-20 — A capability restriction enforced after the fact on a lane that was *provisioned with* the capability
instance: "the lane cannot push — there is a check at the push, a check at the autocommit, a check at PR creation, and a guard at `land`." Each check is real, each is tested, and the count of them reads as depth. the restricted lane is built out of exactly the same materials as the unrestricted one — same writable git worktree, same `origin` remote, same inherited credentials — and only the *checks* differ. Every check then sits at a point the actor can route around, and each round of hardening adds another one at another such point. Measured here across three rounds of the same feature: a `consult_only` dispatch lane was handed a real worktree and policed afterwards; the refusal was walked around first by a harness that committed on its own, then by a `run` template that pushed **during** its own execution (every barrier ran only after the harness process exited), then twice at `land` — once by renaming the hand-pushed branch out of the `dispatch/<task>` namespace so the guard's `if managed` block never ran, and once by passing an explicit `--task` naming an unrelated record so the consult lookup read the wrong one. Three independent bypasses, one shape. treating a restriction as a *policy over behaviour* rather than a *property of the environment*. Any check evaluated after the actor has the capability is a race the actor can win, and a check evaluated *before* is one the actor can reach around. Removing the worktree, branch, remote, and credential makes "cannot push from the provisioned consult root" true of that root. It does **not** make the claim true of an arbitrary same-user process that can name another checkout; that broader guarantee additionally requires a process boundary, supplied for Hermes by its immutable remote transport.
check: when a lane, role, or agent must never do X, ask what it is *given* that makes X possible and remove that, before writing any check that forbids X. Then audit everything the process can reach outside the provisioned lane and add a boundary the contained party cannot replace. Keep the checks — as **invariant asserts** whose firing means your own bookkeeping is broken — but never let them be the mechanism. Test the absence directly (no ref exists, discovery cannot reach the repository, the credential variable is unset in the child process) and test the boundary adversarially (an absolute-path checkout, PATH-shadowed launcher, and SSH `ProxyCommand` must not execute). Prove each assertion is load-bearing by mutating the provisioning or launcher and watching the test fail. Corollary for reviewers: "we added a fourth barrier" is evidence the first three were the wrong shape, not that the fourth is the right one.

source_anchor: CI-21 — A credential-scrub enumeration modeled only the channels that go through config files, and missed the one that doesn't
instance: "push-capable credentials are stripped from the consult harness's environment" — true of every variable that routes through `git`/`gh`'s own config resolution (`GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, the askpass hooks, `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`/`GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM` where `credential.helper` lives), which round 3 of PR #153 (CI-20) enumerated and closed. on a workstation with a real desktop session, `gh`'s OAuth token can live in the OS keyring (GNOME/KDE Secret Service) instead of, or in addition to, `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`. Reading it needs nothing from the scrub above: `secret-tool search service gh:github.com` (libsecret) resolves the credential over the D-Bus **session** bus and never touches `GH_CONFIG_DIR`, git config, or any of the token env vars. Measured on a real session: the call succeeded and returned the stored credential using only `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` to find the bus — a channel absent from every round of the enumeration that produced CI-18, because every prior round reasoned from "how does `git`/`gh` authenticate," not "what can any same-user process reach." an enumeration of "every way to obtain push capability" was scoped to the credential *system under test's own config surface* (git/gh) rather than to *everything a same-user process can reach*. A same-privilege desktop session shares more than the target program's config files — it shares the session bus, the keyring daemon, and whatever else registers on it — and none of that is visible from reading `git`/`gh` source or config alone.
check: when scrubbing an environment to deny a capability, enumerate reachable *channels* (same-user IPC: D-Bus session bus, keyring/agent sockets, shared-memory or well-known-socket services) before enumerating the *target program's* documented config surface — the latter is a subset of the former, not a superset. For the D-Bus/keyring case specifically: unset `DISPLAY`/`XAUTHORITY` (denies X11 session-bus autolaunch) and `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`/`DBUS_STARTER_ADDRESS`/`DBUS_STARTER_BUS_TYPE` (denies direct address), *and* repoint `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` at an empty directory (denies the D-Bus spec's own fallback path, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bus`, which the address-unset step alone does not close). Test the absence with a probe that reproduces the actual resolution order a real client library uses, not just a grep for the credential in a config file.

source_anchor: CI-22 — A repair for a false positive silently inverts the error into a false negative
instance: "the defect is fixed and the tests are green" — when the fix traded a benign wrong answer for the dangerous one, in a detector whose entire job is the dangerous direction. the repair *loosened* a predicate. Repairs are usually written by relaxing whatever fired wrongly, and relaxing is asymmetric — it always moves toward permissive. For any gate, guard, or detector, permissive is the unsafe direction, so the default repair motion points at the worse failure mode. Measured here: `dispatch/tools/dispatch-wave.sh` reported a `committed-no-pr` success as `LAUNCH-FAILED`; the fix let a recognised success `.status` override the raw exit code (`elif [[ "$r" != 0 && "$status_ok" -ne 1 ]]`, then `elif [[ "$status_ok" -eq 1 ]] -> OK`). A lane that printed `committed-no-pr` and was then SIGKILLed (rc=137) now read **OK** — a masking bug in the very tool that exists to catch unaccounted lanes. treating a defect as "the predicate said X, make it stop saying X" rather than "which way should this err, and does the repair preserve that?" A detector's two error directions are not symmetric and must not be traded blindly.
check: for any change to a gate or detector, state explicitly **which way it now errs and whether that is the safe direction**; a repair that only ever loosens is suspect. Brief the verifier to attack the *inversion by name* — a generic "review this" passes it, whereas "does this risk masking a real failure whose JSON claims success?" found it twice independently. Prefer **agreement over override**: require two signals to match (here the exit code must equal the status's documented code, `delivered`->0, `committed-no-pr`->10) and treat disagreement as unaccounted. Overriding one signal with another discards evidence; requiring agreement keeps both. Name the resulting state distinctly (`STATUS-RC-MISMATCH`) rather than folding it into an existing one, so the operator sees *why*.

source_anchor: CI-23 — A regression fixture written in a shape the bug does not occupy passes while the bug survives
instance: "the reported defect now has a test, and it passes" — when the test was authored in a *different shape* from the one the report reproduced, so it never exercised the defect. the reproduction in the report and the fixture in the repo differ in a structural detail that looks cosmetic and is not. Measured here: aifleet#624's Defect 1 reproduced as a **one-line** function, `deploy(){ risky "$@"; exit 0; }`. The repair's own new fixture was written **multi-line** — the shape that already worked — so it went green while the literal one-liner stayed silent. The real gate was a bash filter, `[[ "$trimmed" != "exit 0" ]] && continue`, which only ever considered lines whose *entire* content is `exit 0`; every same-line mask was invisible, function or not. Two review rounds passed before a lens was explicitly forbidden from paraphrasing the repro. a fixture gets written from the *understanding* of the bug rather than transcribed from the *reproduction* of it. Any normalisation applied while transcribing — reformatting, splitting lines, renaming, tidying — can move the input out of the failing class.
check: transcribe the reproduction **verbatim** into the fixture; do not reformat it. Then prove the fixture fails against the parent commit — a regression test that passes before the fix proves nothing. When briefing a reviewer, state the required shapes literally and forbid paraphrase. Corollary: a fixture set authored by the rule's own author is the answer key, not a test — require known-positives written by someone who did not write the rule, and require the *negative* direction too (correct inputs must stay silent), since a rule that fires on everything discriminates no better than one that fires on nothing.

source_anchor: CI-24 — A retraction or correction mechanism is itself an attack surface
instance: "the record is trustworthy because wrong entries can be retracted or corrected" — when the retraction path is the cheapest way to make a true entry disappear. a system gains an amend/retract/supersede/close capability to fix honest mistakes, and nothing distinguishes *correcting an error* from *erasing an inconvenient truth*. The corrective path typically carries lighter authentication and fewer witnesses than the original write, precisely because it is framed as a fix. Ask: who can invoke it, what evidence must accompany it, and is the retraction recorded as durably as the thing retracted? modelling the corrective path as maintenance rather than as a write with the same integrity requirements as any other. An append-only log with an unwitnessed delete is not append-only.
check: hold retractions to the *same or stronger* evidence bar as the original claim, and record the retraction as a new durable entry rather than mutating or removing the old one. Prefer superseding-with-reason over deletion, so the fact that a claim was made and was wrong survives. Where a retraction can be self-issued by the party the record is about, require an unowned witness — [[lesson-containment-needs-an-unowned-boundary]] applies to records, not only to processes.

source_anchor: CI-25 — A tool baked into the CI image but absent from the runner's service PATH makes a suite report zero executed cases
instance: the suite ran and nothing failed — because the runner is the same suite, same command, same repo as CI. `bats --jobs 4` shells out to GNU `parallel`. `parallel` is present in the ARC image, and present on leviathan only under `/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/bin`, which the systemd unit's `Environment=PATH` omitted. Result: `parallel: command not found` and `Executed 0 instead of expected 895`. The **executed-vs-counted gate caught it loudly** — a suite that reports a case count and asserts against it is the positive control that makes this class visible at all. the CI image's implicit tool inventory is not part of any declared contract, so a second execution environment inherits only the tools someone remembered. A dependency that is implicit in the image is invisible to the dependency-verification step.
check: (1) every tool the suite shells out to belongs in the workflow's explicit `Verify required dependencies` list, including ones the image happens to provide; (2) *append* extra directories to a unit's `Environment=PATH` rather than prepending, so nothing already resolvable is shadowed; (3) keep an executed-count floor on every suite — "0 executed" must fail, never pass quietly.

source_anchor: CI-26 — A path filter derived from where a job's entrypoint lives, rather than what the job executes, silently skips required coverage while reporting green
instance: "this PR did not touch that area, so that job did not need to run" — the filter is treated as a statement about coverage when it is only a statement about file location. fleet PR #334 carried **three instances of this one class in a single PR across two adversarial review rounds**: (1) per-job filters omitted cross-tree dependencies the corpora actually load at runtime — `check-gaming`'s fixture copies `dispatch/`, symlinks `routing/`, and copies `orchestration/test/harness.js`, none of which were in its filter; (2) **renames were invisible** — GitHub's compare API reports `filename` (new path) plus `previous_filename` (old path), and only `filename` was read, so `git mv orchestration/src/foo.js docs/foo.js` skipped all four corpus jobs; (3) the `bats` job invoked `ci-gate.bats` **by name**, so any new test file added beside it would never execute. Each review round caught one instance and missed another. the filter was authored from the mental model "where does this job's entrypoint live", not "what does this job read at runtime". Both look identical on a green run, and the failure mode is an *invisible absence* — a job that did not run, a test that did not execute — which review is structurally poor at seeing.
check: derive filters from **executed dependencies** (what the job loads, copies, symlinks, or globs), not entrypoint location; read `previous_filename` as well as `filename` from the compare API; glob test directories rather than naming files. Because two adversarial rounds each missed an instance, **this class is only reliably caught by a committed test, not by a reviewer** — the method change was to extract the filter logic to `.github/scripts/ci-changed-areas.sh` and pin it with `orchestration/test/bats/ci-changed-areas.bats` (19 cases), mutation-verified red across three defect families including the degenerate "widen the filter to match everything" fix.

source_anchor: CI-27 — A job routed to a runner label with no online runner queues indefinitely rather than failing
instance: a misrouted job will error out and tell you. GitHub Actions holds a job in `queued` forever when no runner matches its labels. There is no error, no annotation, and no failure — the PR simply never reports. (Identified as a live trap before routing this session's jobs; not observed as an outage.) label matching is a scheduling filter, not a validity check. "No runner has this label" and "every runner is busy" are the same state to the scheduler.
check: confirm at least one runner with the target label is online *before* routing work to it, and set `timeout-minutes` on every job so a stalled queue fails loudly instead of hanging. A queue with no possible consumer must be made to fail, since it cannot be made to error. the fallback shipped for `leviathan-big` observes leviathan from `homelab-arc`, so **`homelab-arc` itself remains an unobserved single label** — if ARC is down, `changes`, `runner_gate` and every job that needs them queue in exactly this shape. That is not a regression (`changes` has always been ARC-only, and every corpus job already needs it), but it is the same trap one layer down. Closing it needs an observer outside *both* self-hosted fleets — a GitHub-hosted (`ubuntu-latest`) watchdog — which bills against a private repo's 2000 free minutes/month and is therefore a founder spend decision, not a CI-PR decision.

source_anchor: CI-28 — A PR merged at a head that has moved past the reviewed commit ships unreviewed resolution work
instance: "this PR was reviewed and approved" — with approval attached to a commit that is no longer the merged head. fleet PR #322 was reviewed at `bed2ce0` and merged at `f472b00`, after two mechanical conflict resolutions landed on top. Mitigating but **not exculpating:** the conflicts were `REPORT.md`-only and CI was rerun green — the resolution itself was still never reviewed by anyone. the finished-PR gate checks that a review exists, not that it applies to the commit being merged. "Mechanical" is a judgment made by the party doing the resolving.
check: the merge gate must assert `head == reviewed commit`. If the head moved, either re-review the delta or re-run the review at the new head — a green CI rerun proves the tests still pass, not that the resolution was correct.

source_anchor: CI-29 — A guard whose own pinning suite is unguarded
instance: "the pinning suites cannot be silently deleted — the required-suite guard names them." `.github/scripts/orch-bats-suites.sh` requires suites by name so that a deletion fails CI, but its default list names only `ci-gate.bats ci-changed-areas.bats`, while `orchestration/test/bats/` now holds **five** pinning suites. `ci-report-md-guard.bats`, `check-gaming-skip-audit.bats`, and — sharpest — `orch-bats-suites.bats` itself can all be deleted with CI staying green. The guard cannot detect the deletion of its own test. the required list is a hand-maintained enumeration that grew apart from the directory it is supposed to pin. Nothing derives one from the other, and the guard's self-test is not a member of the set it guards.
check: every new pinning suite is added to the required list in the same PR that introduces it, and the guard's own suite is a required member. Better still, derive the required set from the directory and fail on any suite present on disk but absent from the list.

source_anchor: CI-30 — A count gate left above the measured value grants free slack and whitelists the cases it exists to catch
instance: "the skip baseline is a ratchet, so skips can only go down." after the three R6 findings were repaired, measured skips were **0** while `BATS_SKIP_BASELINE` still read `3` and `skip-baseline.txt` still named `R6-AD4b`, `R6-AUD1`, `R6-GATE1`. Two effects: three arbitrary cases could start skipping and stay green, and the *name* gate — the entire anti-net-zero-substitution mechanism — was pre-approving the exact three security regressions it existed to catch. the baseline was treated as a configuration constant rather than as a measurement, so paying down the debt it counted did not touch it. A name-allowlist is strictly worse than a count when stale: it does not merely permit slack, it specifically re-permits the named failures.
check: a baseline is re-measured and lowered in the same change that pays down what it counted; a named-exemption list is emptied by the fix, not left behind as documentation of what used to be broken.

source_anchor: CI-31 — A three-outcome test helper whose middle outcome passes silently against production state
instance: "the helper either isolates the test or skips it, so a green `ok` means the assertions ran under isolation." `dispatch/test/helpers.bash:213-256` `use_isolated_operator_home()` has three modes: bwrap works → full assertions; bwrap unavailable **but** the operator's real `~/.config/cli-dispatch/trusted-reviewers` exists → a read-only pass-through against the **real production trust root**, emitting `ok` with no `# skip`; neither → skip. On the old ARC runner the middle mode was unreachable, so a bwrap regression surfaced as 283 loud skips. On a workstation runner that shares a host with a real operator home, the same regression instead flips ~19 call sites to a weaker-mode **pass** — invisible to the skip-count gate and to the skip-name list, because a degraded pass is still `ok`. the gates observe outcomes (`ok` / `skip`), and the degradation was designed to preserve the outcome while changing the guarantee. Moving runners changed which branch is reachable without changing any test.
check: assert the isolation **mode** as a CI precondition, not just the outcome — fail the job if bwrap user namespaces are unavailable, and make the degraded branch emit `skip` (or hard-fail) rather than `ok`. Any fallback that weakens a guarantee must change the observable signal.

source_anchor: CI-32 — `timeout-minutes` does not bound queue time
instance: "a `timeout-minutes` on the job caps how long the pipeline can be stuck on it." the timer starts when a job is **assigned** to a runner, not when it is queued. A job targeting a label with no online runner sits queued until GitHub's 24-hour limit with the job timeout never arming. Because `cli-dispatch land` refuses to merge on incomplete checks (exit 8), the entire delegated-dispatch pipeline stalls with no error at all — only a pending check. the only timeout control in the workflow measures execution, and the failure being guarded against is non-execution. Nothing in the workflow can observe "no runner will ever pick this up."
check: a label served by a single host needs a fallback label or a documented manual override with an accepted RTO; `timeout-minutes` is not that control. Alert on queue age externally, and treat single-host labels as a declared availability dependency. **Implemented (fleet#368):** `.github/workflows/leviathan-heartbeat.yml` probes the label every 15 min and observes the probe from the *other* fleet, since a queued job emits nothing observable from inside; `.github/scripts/leviathan-health.sh` turns that run history into the label the `bats`/`harness-python` jobs are *created* on (Actions cannot retarget or cancel an already-queued job, so the decision must precede job creation); alerting is a failed default-branch scheduled run, a deduped outage issue, and an in-PR annotation. Two things that look like weaknesses are deliberate and must not be "fixed": the fallback route makes `bats` go **red** on `homelab-arc` (no bwrap userns — see CI-33) rather than lowering `BATS_SKIP_BASELINE`/`BATS_EXECUTED_FLOOR`, and every *undecidable* state keeps the primary route while still alerting, because rerouting on a guess converts "unknown" into a guaranteed failure. Design and rejected alternatives: `dispatch/doc/368-fallback-design.md`.

source_anchor: CI-33 — A dependency preflight that verifies everything except the property the change is premised on
instance: "the job preflights its dependencies, so the host is verified fit for the suite." the bats job verifies `bats node rg jq git patch perl awk parallel` — but not `bwrap`, whose **working user namespaces** are the entire justification both for routing to the new runners and for pruning 283 skip entries. The one property the change was premised on was the one property not checked. the preflight enumerates the tools the suite invokes, which is a list that predates the change; the change's premise was a host capability, and no step existed to add it. Preflights inherit from the past, premises come from the present.
check: when a change is justified by a host property, that property joins the preflight in the same PR that relies on it. State the premise explicitly in the PR and check it mechanically.

source_anchor: CI-34 — A floor left at its old measured value becomes decorative as the corpus grows
instance: "the executed-count floor guards against test deletion." `BATS_EXECUTED_FLOOR: "246"` was measured on ARC; the suite now executes **930** cases. **73% of `dispatch/test` could be deleted and still clear the floor.** The tight `bats_ran != test_count` equality check is sound but derives `test_count` from `bats --count` on the same run, so it cannot see a deletion at all — the floor is the only deletion guard, and it has 684 cases of slack. a floor is an absolute threshold against a growing quantity; it decays into a no-op automatically, without anyone changing it. Its companion check is self-referential and therefore cannot cover the gap.
check: re-measure and raise the floor whenever the corpus grows (ideally mechanically, as a ratchet on the last green run), and add a deletion guard that compares against the committed corpus rather than against the run's own count.

source_anchor: CI-35 — A review finding that names one instance of a class is indistinguishable from one that names the class
instance: "the reviewer found this defect, so the defect is now known and the repair closes it" — where the finding named a single coordinate and the repair fixed exactly that coordinate. an adversarial review reported "the copied `cli-dispatch` cannot find its sourced lib" against `dispatch/test/harness-consult-only.bats`. Three further instances of the identical shape existed — `covariate-lifecycle.bats:34`, `doctor.bats:352`, `doctor.bats:398` — and were caught only by a full-suite run two rounds later. The repair fixed the named file and the hole simply relocated; nothing in the finding's wording distinguished "here is an instance" from "here is the class." a finding's prose carries its severity and its mechanism but not its *cardinality*, and the reader supplies the missing quantifier optimistically. A reviewer who greps one path and a reviewer who swept the tree produce findings that read the same.
check: a finding must state how many coordinates of its shape exist and how that count was obtained (the grep, the glob, the suite run) — or say explicitly that it did not sweep. A repair brief derived from an unswept finding inherits that gap, so treat "swept: no" as a required follow-up step, not a caveat. Where the class is mechanically enumerable, the sweep belongs in a committed test rather than in a reviewer's diligence.

source_anchor: CI-36 — Adding a sourced lib silently breaks every fixture that stages the program bare
instance: "the program is a script, so copying the script stages the program." `dispatch/cli-dispatch` gained a runtime-required sibling (`terminal-state.sh`) and became a two-file program. Five test sites copied the script alone into a temp directory; every invocation from those fixtures died with `cannot find terminal-state.sh`. The refactor's own tests passed, because they ran the program from its real directory — only the fixtures that deliberately relocate it broke, and they broke uniformly. "what the program *is*" was tracked in one place (the repo layout) while "what the program *needs at runtime*" was assumed to be a single file by every consumer. A single-file program has no manifest, so nothing enumerates the sites that stage it, and the invariant lives only in the habits of whoever wrote each fixture.
check: when a program gains a runtime-required sibling file, sweep for *every* site that stages, copies, installs, packages, or symlinks it — tests, install/uninstall paths, Dockerfiles, CI workflow steps, PATH symlinks, and docs that tell a reader to copy it — in the same PR. Fixing only the failing test guarantees the remaining sites fail later and separately. Better: make the program refuse to start with a clear error naming the missing sibling, so a bare copy fails loudly at its first invocation rather than mid-suite.

source_anchor: CI-37 — The guard-hardening treadmill: closing pattern-matcher bypasses needs a parser, not more regex
instance: "one more spelling closed, and the guard is now sound." a grep-based guard against staging `cli-dispatch` without its sibling lib was hardened three times, and every round found new bypass spellings: quote-before-slash, `cat >`, `tar`, variable indirection, backslash line continuation, and a heredoc that writes a copier. Each round genuinely closed what it found and each round left the class open, because the guard was matching surface text against a language with unbounded ways to spell the same operation. a regex over shell source is an approximation of a shell parser, and the gap is not a finite list of holes to enumerate. Compounding it, this guard was defense-in-depth over a check that already fails correctly — a lib-less copy fails its own test — so each hardening round bought a shrinking amount of real protection at a constant cost.
check: decide up front whether the guard is the primary check or defense-in-depth. If a downstream check already fails on the real condition, stop hardening the pattern matcher at the first bypass round and document the limitation honestly instead of implying coverage the guard does not have. If it *is* the primary check, escalate the mechanism — parse, or observe the effect (does the staged directory contain the sibling?) rather than the source text that would produce it. An "N rounds of new bypasses" trace is a signal to change the mechanism, not to write round N+1.

source_anchor: CI-38 — A safety bound derived from a constant's declaration rather than from its callers
instance: "the watchdog's grace period comfortably exceeds the longest legitimate absence, because `MAX_WAIT=2400`." the leviathan runner watchdog assumed `MAX_WAIT=2400` (40 minutes) bounded how long a Listener could legitimately be absent, and set a 45-minute grace against it. `MAX_WAIT` is per-*sleep*, not per-start: `run-ephemeral.sh` calls the wait at the top of every `gh_retry` attempt (up to 5) and twice per start, so the legitimate worst case is roughly **6.8 hours** against a 45-minute grace. The bound was asserted in the design note, encoded in the code, *and* pinned by a committed bats assertion — three artifacts agreeing, all three wrong, because all three read the declaration. a constant's name and value describe one invocation; the safety property is about the *aggregate* across the call graph. Restating the same misread in a second and third artifact produces the appearance of corroboration while adding no independent check — the design note, the code, and the test all had one upstream source.
check: trace a safety bound to the **callers** of the constant — count invocations along the worst-case path (retry loops, nested waits, per-attempt calls) — and record the derivation next to the bound so the next reader can falsify it. A test that asserts the same number the code declares is not a check; the test must assert the aggregate, computed independently. When a bound guards a destructive action (here: restarting a runner mid-job), require the derivation before the action ships.

source_anchor: CI-39 — "Cannot observe" collapsed into "confirmed absent," so a probe outage reads as a fleet-wide fault
instance: the probe returned *absent*, therefore the thing is absent. `watchdog.sh:84-96` `has_listener()` returns *absent* for three distinguishable situations: a genuine miss, an unreadable cgroup, and an empty `ControlGroup` field. A systemic probe failure — a permissions change, a systemd field rename, a cgroup layout change — would therefore mark **all four healthy runners as stalled simultaneously** and restart them mid-job. Sharpest detail: the sibling file `decide.sh` in the same codebase holds the "unknown never resolves to fine" line correctly, so one author got the three-state distinction right in one file and lost it in the next. a boolean return type has no room for the third state, and the negative branch is the one that happens to be reachable when the probe breaks. The failure is also *correlated* — a probe outage hits every subject at once — so the resulting action is not one wrong restart but a simultaneous fleet-wide one, which is exactly the shape a health check exists to prevent.
check: probe failure is a third state and must be represented as one — `present` / `absent` / `unknown` — with `unknown` never collapsing into the branch that authorizes action. Where a health check drives a destructive remediation, `unknown` must suppress the action and alarm. When two files in one codebase implement the same three-state rule, extract it rather than restating it; the correct implementation existing next door is not protection.

source_anchor: MDL-20 — Two agent lanes reach opposite conclusions; the tiebreaker is which one held the data, not which argued better
instance: an agent's stated conclusion is evidence for that conclusion. two subagent lanes investigating the same question — was fleet CI slowed by cgroup CPU throttling? — returned **opposite** verdicts with comparable confidence and comparable prose quality. The lane holding direct measurement (`nr_throttled` from live pods) was right; the lane reasoning from a `requests/limits` comment in `ci.yml` was wrong. Nothing in either report's *form* distinguished them. confidence and articulacy are uncorrelated with whether the agent ever touched the data that would settle the question. A conclusion reported without its measurement is indistinguishable from a conclusion reported with one.
check: when lanes disagree, do not weigh the arguments — ask which lane executed the query that could falsify its own claim, and demand the artifact (counter values, command output, diff). A lane that cannot show the measurement loses to one that can, regardless of reasoning quality. Brief lanes to state explicitly what they measured versus what they inferred.

source_anchor: MDL-21 — A security warning that describes an action which was actually blocked
instance: the monitor reported the action, therefore the action happened. a subagent-monitor warning reported that `helm upgrade` had been applied to ten shared scale sets. Direct verification showed the live pods still carried `requests.cpu: "1"` and every helm release's last deploy predated the run — the permission classifier had **denied** the apply, and the warning described the *attempt*. Acting on the warning without verifying would have triggered an unnecessary rollback against a production cluster. monitors observe intents (tool calls issued) rather than effects (state changed), and a denial leaves the intent record intact. A high-urgency framing then makes the un-verified claim likelier to be acted on immediately, which is exactly when verification is skipped.
check: a warning is a claim; confirm it against the live system before remediating — especially when the remediation is itself a production write. Remediation of an alert is a destructive action and inherits the evidence bar of one.

source_anchor: OPS-51 — Backgrounded `codex exec` without stdin redirect blocks forever on the stdin banner
instance: a backgrounded `codex exec` invocation is believed to be running the task; it prints progress-looking output and a running process is visible, so it reads as working, just slow. the output file prints "Reading additional input from stdin..." and then goes silent — frozen at that banner indefinitely, because non-interactive `codex exec` without `< /dev/null` blocks waiting for stdin that a backgrounded process will never receive. Measured 2026-07-31: one run left backgrounded without stdin redirect ran 1h29m, produced 39 bytes of output, and was killed; an identical run with `< /dev/null` completed in ~10 minutes.
check: every non-interactive `codex exec` invocation gets `< /dev/null` (or an equivalent explicit empty-stdin redirect), always — especially when backgrounded. If an output file is frozen at the stdin banner, that is the tell: kill it and relaunch with the redirect rather than waiting longer.

source_anchor: OPS-52 — Empty-label kubectl delete with a phase filter sweeps the whole namespace, not just the intended pods
instance: "cleaning up my test pods" — believed a phase filter (`--field-selector=status.phase=Succeeded`) scoped the delete to pods this session created. `kubectl delete pods --field-selector=status.phase=Succeeded -n <ns>` carried no label selector at all, so it matched **every** Succeeded pod in the namespace, not just the ones from this run. Two unrelated terminal pods belonging to other work were deleted on 2026-08-08 during ARC-runner bwrap userns cleanup. a phase filter narrows by pod *state*, not by pod *ownership*. With no label selector, "Succeeded" is satisfied by anything in the namespace that happens to be done, including other sessions' finished jobs.
check: always name cleanup pods explicitly (`kubectl delete pod <name1> <name2> ...`) or scope by a lane-specific label applied at creation time (`kubectl delete pods -l run=<session-id>`) — never combine a bare phase filter with an empty label selector as the sole scoping mechanism.

source_anchor: OPS-53 — Dispatcher-yield stall: external background work has no hook for re-invocation when it finishes
instance: a dispatcher subagent's "waiting" status is expected to resolve when background work it launched finishes, because there is somewhere to notify when progress arrives. a coordinator-spawned dispatcher subagent ends its turn with `status: waiting`, claiming it is armed to resume when one of its dispatch lanes finishes. The lane is external (a bare `cli-dispatch` setsid process, a Monitor that has already fired, or a purely aspirational intention to wait). None of these integrate with the harness's event system: no callback can fire, the dispatcher sleeps forever, and all downstream lanes finish unwatched. Observed 3x on 2026-08-08 across three different dispatcher instances (273-chain-B, throughput-fixes builder, review-317/323 dispatcher); each required manual coordinator intervention to resume. a dispatcher may yield intending to be re-invoked when something finishes, but the yieldable thing must be a harness-resident background task (`Monitor`, a `background: true` subagent) registered in the harness's own tracking. An external PID, a lane whose run is already complete, or a bare intention to wait are *not* tied to any re-invocation mechanism — the dispatcher is abandoned, not suspended.
check: a dispatcher must never yield without either (1) a terminal receipt confirming work is done, or (2) a **verified live** harness background child (a `Monitor` or `background` task) actually armed to re-invoke it. Verify by the task's own token, not by confidence in the brief. On the coordinator side: any dispatcher completion notification whose result text says "waiting" is a stall, not progress — escalate and do not re-dispatch until the stalled instance is destroyed and the background work accounted for.

source_anchor: OPS-54 — Ephemeral runner couples its uptime to a rate-limited credential shared with everything else on the box
instance: an ephemeral runner is self-sustaining — it registers, runs one job, exits, and the supervisor brings up a fresh one indefinitely. `leviathan-2` picked up a CI job, ran it, and exited (correct ephemeral behavior). Re-registration then needed a fresh registration token, which was minted with founder OAuth — 5000/hr, shared with every other tool on the workstation, and already exhausted. The unit exited 1, systemd restarted it, ten times in five minutes, and the crashloop brake put it in `failed`. **The failure state is unreachable without success:** the sibling runner that never received a job sat in "Listening for Jobs" and looked healthy all night. the token spend is per-registration, i.e. per-job, and it draws on a *shared* exhaustible quota rather than a budget scoped to the runner. Throughput itself is the load that breaks the unit, so the busiest runner fails first and the idle one is reported healthy.
check: (1) preflight the rate limit before minting and sleep until reset (bounded — cap the sleep, then fail loudly rather than sleeping forever); (2) exponential backoff over several attempts instead of instant systemd restart; (3) cache the registration token keyed on the API's own `expires_at`, which converts spend from per-job to per-hour; (4) widen the crashloop window so backoff can complete inside it (5min → 30min). The durable fix is to stop sharing the budget at all — give the GitHub App self-hosted-runner admin so registration draws on the App's separate quota (NOT applied; needs founder authorization).

source_anchor: OPS-55 — A brief that routes round-notes into a shared changelog makes every PR conflict with every other PR
instance: the round-notes file is harmless bookkeeping riding along with the diff; seven lanes each producing merge conflicts looks like seven independent lane mistakes. on 2026-08-09 five fleet PRs (#323, #305, #301, #330, #317) sat DIRTY against main for days. `git merge-tree` showed their **only** conflict was `REPORT.md`; every actual code hunk auto-merged. One had four separate `REPORT.md` conflicts and zero real ones. All five rebased and landed the same day once the `REPORT.md` hunk was dropped. Separately #326 was reconciled against a moving main three times — its `REPORT.md` change was +232/-292 and *overwrote an unrelated prior report*, regenerating the conflict each round; its re-cut (#335) applied to current main with zero conflict. **one briefing defect repeated seven times, not seven lane mistakes.** Instructing lanes to write round-notes into a shared changelog *as part of a code PR* guarantees an N×N conflict matrix independent of lane quality — every lane writes the same path, so N concurrent lanes produce N-1 guaranteed conflicts in a file no gate reads.
check: a lane must never write to the shared `REPORT.md` in a PR that touches code. Findings go in the PR body, or in a per-lane file that cannot collide (`REPORT-<lane>.md`); a separate docs-only PR that lands alone is also fine. Briefs must name that destination explicitly — see BC-11 in `DISPATCH-BRIEF-CHECKLIST.md`. Enforced by the CI guard `.github/scripts/ci-report-md-guard.sh`. When a conflict pattern appears across many lanes at once, audit the brief before auditing the lanes.

source_anchor: OPS-56 — Reconciling against a moving main is an unterminating loop; the fix is a re-cut, not another reconcile
instance: one more conflict resolution will land it. PR #326 was reconciled three times and main advanced during each round, regenerating conflicts every time. The loop only broke on a **re-cut from current main**: PR #335 applied cleanly with zero conflict once the shared `REPORT.md` rewrite was dropped. reconcile is a fixed-point operation against a target that is still moving. When the branch's conflicting surface is large and shared (see OPS-55), the fixed point is never reached.
check: cap reconcile at two rounds; the second same-class conflict is evidence the *approach* is wrong. Re-cut the change from current main, dropping the shared-file surface, rather than resolving a third time. This is the loop-cap rule applied to merge conflicts: hitting the cap forces a method change, not another attempt.

source_anchor: OPS-57 — A PR title advertising a change the PR does not contain sends downstream work hunting for a nonexistent hunk
instance: the title describes the diff. fleet PR #326's title said "raise bats `--jobs`". No file in the PR contains a `--jobs` edit. The work was an *investigation* that concluded do-not-change, written up in `REPORT.md` — a legitimate outcome described by an illegitimate title. Cost: a re-cut lane went looking for a hunk that never existed. the title was written from the task assigned, not from the diff produced. An investigation whose conclusion is "no change" still needs a title that says so.
check: title from the diff, not the assignment. Investigations that conclude do-not-change get an explicit `investigate:`/`docs:` prefix and a title naming the conclusion. A title asserting a code change with no matching hunk should be caught at review.

source_anchor: OPS-58 — Diagnosing from a code comment instead of the live system
instance: the config describes the system, so reading the config is as good as measuring it. the CPU-throttling hypothesis for fleet's 9x CI slowdown was reasoned entirely from a `requests: 1, limits: 4` comment in `ci.yml`. Direct measurement disproved it outright: `nr_throttled 0` / `throttled_usec 0` across ~39,600 quota periods on six live pods. The real cause was **node size** — all 12 k3s nodes are 4-vCPU VMs (48 vCPU total), not the assumed 40-core host, so `requests: cpu 1` let the scheduler pack three runners onto one 4-core node (worker132 PSI `some avg300=55.66`). three successive hypotheses (host contention → cgroup throttling → node sizing) were each generated from a description of the system rather than from the system. The founder's own premise (40 cores, 256GB) was also wrong: the cores existed but were partitioned into twelve 4-vCPU slices, so every layer's *description* was locally plausible and jointly wrong.
check: measure the mechanism you are blaming before proposing a fix for it — throttle counters, PSI, actual node capacity — not the manifest that describes it. A config value states an intent; only the counter states an outcome.

source_anchor: OPS-59 — Deleting a stacked PR's base branch auto-closes the child instead of retargeting it
instance: "GitHub retargets dependent PRs when their base branch is deleted, so `--delete-branch` is safe on a stack." squash-merging fleet #343 with `--delete-branch` left #344 at `state=CLOSED` with its base still pointing at the deleted branch. The PR's content was intact and every check was green — only the base pointer died. `gh pr reopen` was then refused by a permission classifier, so the whole 5-PR stack stalled with no defect in any of the code. GitHub's auto-retarget applies only to PRs based on a branch that was merged *into* their own base in the same operation; a squash-merge plus branch delete drops the ref out from under the child, and a PR whose base ref no longer exists is closed, not moved. The merge command's convenience flag silently owns the fate of every PR stacked above it.
check: merge stacked PRs **without** `--delete-branch`; delete the branches afterwards, once the child PRs have been explicitly retargeted (`gh pr edit --base`). Treat "does anything base on this branch?" as a precondition of any branch deletion.

source_anchor: OPS-60 — A branch cut from an older main reverts merged work if it is retargeted rather than rebased
instance: "the branch only adds my change, so pointing it at main is a no-op for everything else." the `recut/333*` branches were cut from `0c4f9d0` while main had moved on to `11cd693`. Opening a PR from them to main showed **739 deletions** — the merge would have reverted `read-worktree.js`, `skip-baseline.txt`, and `ci.yml`. Caught only because the branch was diffed against current main *before* the PR was opened. retargeting changes the merge base to the fork point, so every commit that landed on main after the cut appears in the diff as a deletion. The branch is not "just my change" — it is a snapshot of an older tree.
check: never retarget a stale branch; rebase it onto current main and then verify the resulting `--stat` against a known expected shape. A diffstat with deletions you cannot name is a stop condition, not a merge conflict to resolve later.

source_anchor: OPS-61 — A parser written against the one format its author had observed
instance: "the API returns ISO 8601, and this parser handles ISO 8601." token-caching code used `jq`'s `fromdateiso8601`, which accepts **only** `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ`. OAuth returns exactly that shape; the GitHub App returns a local offset with fractional seconds (`2026-08-09T03:09:52.807-04:00`). `jq` aborted the entire script with exit 5 and both self-hosted runners crashlooped. the format assumption was taken from a single observed sample, and the strictest available parser was chosen for a field with two producers. A hard abort on an unparseable optimization input turned a cache miss into a service outage.
check: parse timestamps with `date -d`, which handles both shapes, and treat an unparseable value as "do not cache" rather than as a fatal error. A caching layer must degrade to *not caching*, never to *not running*.

source_anchor: OPS-62 — A comment that inverts its meaning after the change it describes
instance: the comment next to the code describes the code. `ci.yml:98-104` still read "the land family skips wholesale on homelab-arc… do not read the land family's CI green as coverage" **after** the routing change made that green into real coverage — the single most valuable thing the change bought. A reader trusting the comment discounts sound evidence and re-does work already proven. explanatory comments are treated as prose, so no gate falsifies them; a change that inverts a comment's truth value leaves it in place, and its authority survives its accuracy. Stale warnings are worse than stale docs because they actively suppress correct conclusions.
check: treat an explanatory comment as an assertion that must be updated or deleted by the change that falsifies it — include comments in the change's own diff review, and prefer comments that name a checkable condition over ones that state a standing conclusion.

source_anchor: OPS-63 — An undeclared production resource drifts because it is absent from every list
instance: "the repo enumerates the estate, so the docs and the upgrade loop cover everything running." `arc-runners-hindsight` is live in the cluster with **no values file in the repo**, pinned to the stale `arc-runner:2.334.0-fleet5` while all ten of its siblings run `fleet9`, and absent from the README's upgrade loop — which is precisely why it drifted. Both `arc/README.md` and `kubernetes/CLAUDE.md` claim ten scale sets; there are **eleven**. every maintenance mechanism iterated over the declared set, so a resource created outside declaration was structurally invisible to upgrades, to blast-radius estimates, and to the docs that were themselves derived from the declared set. The undeclared resource is the one that never gets fixed.
check: enumerate from the **cluster**, not from the doc, when computing blast radius; add a reconciliation check that diffs live releases against declared values files and fails on either direction of mismatch.

source_anchor: OPS-64 — Two lanes independently registered the same incident under the same ID because neither checked the registry first
instance: picking the next free ID number is enough due diligence before appending a new entry. `FAILURE-MODES.md` carried two separate `### OPS-55` headings with different bodies describing the *same* incident from two angles (the shared-`REPORT.md` conflict campaign — PRs #323/#305/#301/#330/#317, plus #326's three reconciles) — one lane wrote the briefing-defect framing, the other wrote the merge-tree evidence, and neither found the other's entry before appending. the registry's collision check was "is this ID number free," not "does this incident already have an entry." Two lanes working the same incident independently both passed that check because they looked at ID numbers, not at content.
check: before appending a new entry, grep the registry for the incident's distinguishing evidence (PR numbers, error strings, tool/file names) — not just for a free ID number. A duplicate ID is the symptom; a duplicate *incident* under different IDs would be just as bad and this check catches both.

source_anchor: OPS-65 — `git cherry` cannot see squash merges, so it reports landed work as unmerged
instance: "`git cherry` says these commits are not in main, so this branch holds genuinely unmerged work." `git cherry` compares **patch-ids**. A squash merge rewrites the patch, so every commit on a squash-merged branch keeps reporting as `+` (unmerged) forever. Measured: `7257a09` on `ci/optimize-2026-08` was confidently reported as unmerged work; both of its features — the `changes` path-filter job and the cached `install-bats-ripgrep` action — were already present in main, having arrived by squash merge. ancestry and patch-identity are both proxies for the question actually being asked, which is "does this content exist on main?" A squash merge deliberately breaks both proxies, and the tool's output is confident rather than uncertain, so the wrong answer arrives with no hedge attached.
check: after any squash-merge workflow, decide branch disposition by **content**, not ancestry — for each feature the branch claims, check whether it exists on main (`git grep` the identifying string, diff the file, read the workflow). Use `git cherry` and `--merged` only as a first-pass filter that can produce false "unmerged" verdicts, never as the disposition itself. Check for stashes on the branch before deleting it.

source_anchor: OPS-66 — A process was killed on inferred ownership, not verified ownership
instance: "that lane finished, so this `bats` process is its orphan and I can clean it up." the coordinator killed PID 3896788 believing it an orphan of a finished lane. It was a live lane's in-flight suite, and the evidence is unmistakable — a complete, passing TAP body followed by `BATS_EXIT=143`. Ownership was never checked against the live lane set; it was inferred from the coordinator's own stale belief about which lanes had ended. on this host a `pkill -f bats` would additionally have reached the **in-flight CI job on `leviathan-2`**, which runs bats out of `~/actions-runners/work/`, because a self-hosted runner shares the process table with every session on the box. **This command was never run;** the reachability is established by where the runner executes bats, not by an observed kill. It is logged here as a hazard the same root cause implies, not as an incident that occurred. ownership was inferred rather than checked. A name pattern makes this strictly worse — it selects by *what a process is* when the question that matters is *whose it is*, and on this host two independent owners hide behind one pattern (other agent lanes, and the self-hosted runner's work tree) — but the measured failure needed no name pattern to happen. Stale belief about lane state was sufficient.
check: kill by PID only, never by name pattern, and before killing confirm the PID's ownership — check its working directory and ancestry against live lane worktrees and against any runner work directory (`~/actions-runners/work/`). "I believe that lane finished" is not ownership evidence; verify the lane is terminal first. A `143` exit following a complete passing body is the signature of this failure and should be read as "someone killed a healthy run," not as a test failure.

source_anchor: OPS-67 — Concurrent local suites on the CI host make every measurement, in both directions, uninterpretable
instance: "running the suite locally while CI runs gives me a faster read on the same question." three concurrent 1009-case runs on one 48-thread workstation, alongside the real CI job on the same box. One collapsed with `Executed 40 instead of expected 930`; another emitted **7 TAP lines in 45 minutes**. Neither outcome was evidence of anything: the failure did not indicate a defect and the absence of failures elsewhere did not indicate health. The contention also degrades the CI job the runs were meant to inform. the suite's own isolation machinery (temp dirs, sandboxes, timeouts, process budgets) is provisioned per-run, so N concurrent runs contend for resources the tests treat as exclusive. Contention manifests as *test-shaped* symptoms — truncated execution, stalls, timeouts — which are indistinguishable from real defects in the output, so the noise is not merely uninformative but actively misleading.
check: do not run a local full suite on a host while CI is running on it; queue instead. If a contended run is unavoidable, isolate `TMPDIR` per run, cap concurrency at one, and **state in the report that the measurement was contended** so no downstream reader treats it as evidence. A run showing `executed < expected` is void, not red.

source_anchor: ORC-17 — The coordinator's own unverified diagnosis is dispatched as a settled premise
instance: "the root cause is known, the agents only have to implement the fix" — when the cause was read off the source and never reproduced. the dispatch brief contains a phrase like *"already diagnosed by the coordinator — do not re-derive, verify then fix"*, and no artifact backs it: no reproduction, no instrumented run, no failing-then-passing measurement. Measured here: a flaky liveness test was attributed to "cli-dispatch startup exceeding the test's fixed 250ms delay, so the FIRST sample already reads the updated value". Plausible, consistent with the symptom, and unconfirmed. When finally measured, the flake reproduced 10/12 under real concurrent-agent load but **0/10 under synthetic CPU load** and 0/15 quiet — so the stated mechanism was not established, and the brief had frozen a guess as the specification. the coordinator is the one role no reviewer audits. A finding from a subagent gets adversarially verified; a finding the coordinator produces goes straight into the next brief wearing the same confident register. Telling agents *not* to re-derive removes the last check.
check: mark epistemic status in every brief — *measured* / *inferred from code* / *hypothesis*. Never write "do not re-derive" over anything unreproduced; instead say "hypothesis, confirm before fixing". Prefer fixes that are **robust to the diagnosis being wrong** (here, a monotonically advancing counter fixes the test under *any* timing ordering) — and when you take that route, say explicitly that it also **masks** the defect if the cause turns out not to be timing.

source_anchor: ORC-18 — A plugin-bridge subagent's returned job/run ID never registers in its own job registry
instance: a codex-rescue / grok-delegate plugin-bridge subagent hands back a background job or run ID, and the coordinator trusts that ID as proof the work is dispatched and tracked — the ID *looks* like a real handle, so "dispatched" reads as "running, and findable later." querying the job registry immediately after dispatch shows the returned ID absent — nothing was ever actually registered under it. A coordinator that doesn't check this reports the delegated work as done (or as "in progress, check back") when it never ran at all — same shape as ORC-10 (a launch receipt mistaken for a result).
check: query the relevant job registry right after dispatch and confirm the bridge-returned ID is present before relying on it for anything — status checks, completion claims, or downstream work gated on the job. Until confirmed, treat the ID as unverified. Prefer direct CLI invocation (`codex exec`, `grok -p`) over the plugin bridge when the task's correctness depends on being able to track or verify it later.

source_anchor: ORC-19 — A subagent proves an auth channel exists by retrieving the credential, materializing it into a transcript or file
instance: "the credential-scrub was verified — I confirmed the channel is reachable" — where *confirming* meant reading the live secret into tool output. an agent asked to enumerate how a restricted process could still obtain credentials demonstrates reachability the most direct way available, and the value lands in a transcript, a scratch file, or a downstream prompt. Measured twice in one session, both during legitimate work: (1) an agent enumerating push channels for a consult-only lane ran `secret-tool search service gh:github.com` and printed the live OAuth token into its own transcript; (2) an agent setting up git auth wrote a live GitHub App installation token in plaintext to `/tmp/netrc-aifleet` at mode **664 (world-readable)** on a shared host, then embedded it in a follow-up agent prompt — that second hop was blocked by a safety classifier, which killed an unrelated verification lane as collateral. "prove the channel is reachable" and "retrieve the secret" are not the same task, but the second is the obvious way to accomplish the first, and nothing in a normal brief separates them. Reachability is a property of the *path*, not of the *value*.
check: brief any agent enumerating credential channels to establish reachability **without materializing the secret** — check that the socket/daemon/keyring entry responds, compare a hash or a length, or observe an authenticated call succeed, but never print, echo, or write the value. Forbid writing credentials to files at all; where a helper genuinely needs one, use a process-scoped env var, never a file. Where an agent must be handed a token, treat its transcript as compromised for that token's lifetime and rotate. Note the second-order cost: a classifier correctly blocking propagation can silently drop a downstream verification step, so re-do that verification by hand rather than assuming it ran.

source_anchor: ORC-20 — A merge auto-closes an issue tracking the gap the PR deliberately left open
instance: the issue tracker says a gap is resolved because a related PR merged, when that PR's own text states it does not close it. an issue filed *from* a PR's residual-scope section gets referenced in that PR's body, and the merge closes it by keyword or linkage. The closure looks authoritative — right repo, right timing, bot-authored — and is exactly wrong. Measured here: fleet#167 (consult-only lanes have no OS-level isolation) was auto-closed when PR#153 merged, though #153's Scope section says verbatim that it does *not* deliver OS-level isolation. Re-verified at the merged head: still zero isolation primitives in `cli-dispatch`. issue linkage encodes *relatedness*, not *resolution*, but the close action treats them as identical. Note the perverse incentive: a PR that honestly documents its own residual gap is *more* likely to reference that issue, so honesty raises the risk.
check: after merging any PR that references an issue it does not resolve, re-check that issue's state. Prefer wording that cannot trigger auto-close ("tracked as #N", "residual gap: #N") and audit closures whose only evidence is a merge event. Generally: an issue closed by automation carries no evidence — treat a bot-authored close as unverified until the artifact is checked, the same standard applied to any other claim.

source_anchor: ORC-21 — A stated invariant the code never resolves: premise diversity keyed on the ROLE, not the reviewer
instance: a loop that fans out N premise-diverse lenses is believed to produce N independent reviews, because the file says so in a header comment ("vary the premise, not the reviewer"). the model is resolved by ROLE, once — `configuredModel(model, 'attack')` inside a per-lens `map`, with `lens` not even a parameter. The *prompt* varies per lens; the *reviewer* is one actor for all of them. Grep for `independence`/`serving_family`/`model_actual` in the loop and the land gate and get zero hits: nothing computes or records independence, so N correlated reviews are counted as N. Worse than "N lanes on 1 artifact" — this is N prompts on 1 model, and their agreement is reported as corroboration. Varying the model *alias* does not fix it either: three anthropic aliases are one reviewer. the invariant lived in a comment, where nothing executes it. A per-iteration call that *looks* parameterized (it is inside the `map`) reads as if it varies with the loop variable when its arguments do not mention it.
check: resolve the actor per **slot** (lens / voter), compute independence by **serving family** (provider), record it on the result, and make the clean-sweep verdict *depend* on it — a `pass` from an unattested or single-family panel is not evidence of absence, so refuse to report it (prior art: `every-marketplace`'s cross-model review skips the pass when the host's serving family is unattested rather than proceeding and calling it independent). Keep the gate one-directional: it may move pass -> fail, never fail -> pass, and it must never suppress or downgrade a finding — a "fix" that drops findings from a non-independent panel converts a false failure into a false success. Generally: when a doc asserts a property, either mechanize it or mark it aspirational; an unenforced invariant asserted as fact reads as a guarantee to every later reader.

source_anchor: ORC-22 — A recovery path whose blast radius exceeds its mandate manufactures the very failure it recovers from
instance: a cleanup fallback is harmless because it only removes state that is already stale. `orchestration/src/read-worktree.js` `removeWorktree` fell back to a repo-wide `git worktree prune` in order to clean up **one** worktree. `prune` scans and deletes admin state across all of `$GIT_DIR/worktrees/*`, including a sibling directory that a concurrent `worktree add` was mid-write into — producing exactly the `fatal: failed to read .git/worktrees/<id>/commondir: Success` race the fallback existed to recover from. unit-scoped intent implemented with a shared-namespace operation. Under concurrency, "stale" and "half-written" are indistinguishable to a sweeper that has no ownership information.
check: scope every cleanup to the specific unit — read the worktree's own `gitdir:` pointer and delete only that admin directory; add a bounded retry (3 attempts, 25/50ms) on an explicit list of transient patterns; keep the repo-wide sweep only as a genuine last resort behind that. Generally: any recovery that operates on a shared namespace with unit-scoped intent is a race generator, not a recovery.

source_anchor: ORC-23 — An autonomous review lane treats PR/issue comments as part of its work, breaching the publishing gate
instance: a standing merge authorization covers everything a review lane does on the way to merging. a prior-session lane posted review-verdict comments and issue-closing comments to GitHub (fleet#273 items 13, 14) with no founder confirmation. Merges were covered by a standing ruling; **PR and issue comments were not** — they are outbound publishing to an external party and stay gated. the lane generalized "you may merge" into "you may act on GitHub". Authority traces only to the words of the authorization; a comment is an outbound publish regardless of how routine it feels inside the workflow.
check: every dispatch brief explicitly bars comment-posting unless the founder authorized that specific publish. Treat any write that becomes visible to a party outside the session as gated by default, and never infer publishing authority from merge authority.

source_anchor: ORC-24 — A review that exists only in conversation is invisible to the merge gate
instance: "these PRs were reviewed" — where the review lives in a chat transcript no gate can read. fleet PRs #334 and #336 were thoroughly reviewed, then **skipped by an automated merge sweep** for having "no review artifact at head" — while an unreviewed bundled PR merged through a different path. The review work was real and bought nothing; the unreviewed change shipped. review quality was produced in a medium the automation cannot inspect, so the gate's view of the world was exactly inverted relative to the truth. Mechanized trust can only count what is committed.
check: reviews are committed as `REVIEW-<pr>-<reviewer>.md` at the reviewed head, or they do not exist. A review that is not addressable by commit is not an input to any gate.

source_anchor: ORC-25 — Coordinator-as-executor drift
instance: "it was faster to just do this one myself." the coordinator executed work directly instead of dispatching it — systemd/unit edits, plus two PRs authored and merged end to end with no independent review, and direct git operations. Measured cost: a rerun issued from **stale in-context state** consumed scarce runner capacity that a queued PR was waiting on — a dispatched lane holding its own fresh state would not have issued it. It also produced ORC-24 (self-authored, self-merged, unreviewed). the coordinator's context is optimized for adjudication, not execution: it is long-lived, so its view of the tree is stale, and it is the party whose independence the review gate depends on. Every step it executes both risks acting on stale state and removes the only reviewer.
check: the coordinator adjudicates artifacts; execution is dispatched. If a task feels too small to dispatch, that is a signal about dispatch overhead, not a licence to execute — and it never applies to work that must be reviewed.

source_anchor: ORC-26 — The coordinator inverted its own plan's priority order and nothing detected it
instance: "work is proceeding according to the plan" — while the plan's own phase gate was being skipped. the campaign plan stated that CI health lands **first and alone**, because it gates every other lane. The coordinator instead spent five rounds on a Phase 4.0 refactor before starting Phase 1's #368. Nothing in the harness noticed: no gate, no lane, no reviewer — **the founder asked**, and that is how it surfaced. a phase gate written in prose is enforced only by the reader's memory of it, and the coordinator is the reader least able to audit itself — it holds the plan in the same context it holds every distraction, and out-of-order work always has a locally good reason. There is no artifact whose state changes when the order is violated, so there is nothing for any check to read.
check: when a plan declares a phase gate, starting work outside the gated phase requires **stating why the gate does not apply**, in writing, before the work begins — an explicit waiver, not a silent reordering. Bind the gate to something observable: the gating item is an issue that must be closed (or explicitly waived) before dependent lanes are dispatched, so the ordering is a precondition a dispatch can check rather than a paragraph a coordinator can forget.
